svg.title: the framework repairs its own GitLab setup when something breaks it — init heals a revoked token, a tampered variable and a duplicate token, and reload puts a drifted project back
svg.text: the framework repairs its own GitLab setup when
Scenario: init heals a revoked token, a tampered variable and a duplicate token, and reload puts a drifted
A tampered variable and a duplicate token are repaired
A project that drifted is put back in one command

g.text: Given a project the framework has already set up with its automation
token
A fresh project after its first `task devsecops:init`: the access-tokens page shows the
automation token init created.
When the developer revokes the automation token behind the framework's
back
The token is revoked from outside the framework, as if someone deleted it in GitLab: the
access-tokens page no longer lists the automation token.
And the developer runs the framework's init again
A single `task devsecops:init` re-run: the finishing message shows it noticed the token was
missing and created a new one.
Then GitLab now holds a brand-new automation token
The access-tokens page shows the automation token again, a different one from the token that
was revoked.
And GitLab's CI/CD variable now matches the new token
The CI/CD variables page shows the variable again, now pointing at the new token.
And the healed token clones the repository over HTTPS
The healed token signs in to GitLab and lists the repository over HTTPS (the secret and
commit IDs are masked).
When the developer runs init a second time
A second `task devsecops:init` on the already-healed project: the finishing message reports
the token is already in place, nothing to recreate.
Then the second run leaves the healed token untouched
The access-tokens page has not changed: still one automation token. init does not quietly
replace the token on every run.
Given a project the framework already set up and is healthy
A fresh project after its first `task devsecops:init`, working correctly: one automation
token on the access-tokens page.
When a duplicate automation token is planted behind the framework's
back
A second token with the same name is created from outside the framework: the access-tokens
page now lists two automation tokens where there should be one.
And the CI/CD variable is overwritten with a bad value
The CI/CD variable is tampered with, its value replaced by a bad string that GitLab hides on
screen: the CI/CD variables page still lists it.
And the developer runs the framework's init once more
A single `task devsecops:init` re-run: the finishing message shows it removed the duplicate
token and put the CI/CD variable back.
Then only one automation token survives the purge
The access-tokens page is back to a single automation token — the duplicate is gone.
And the healed CI/CD variable clones the repository again
The variable no longer carries the bad value: it signs in to GitLab again and lists the
repository (the secret and commit IDs are masked).
Given a project the framework set up, carrying both its automation
tokens
A project the framework set up on install day: the access-tokens page lists the two
automation tokens it created, one for the release, one for the dependency robot.
And someone loosened its default branch by hand
Someone went into the settings and loosened the default branch by hand: maintainers may push
to it again, which the toolbox never leaves that way.
And a framework file was edited in place
And a framework file was edited in the copy on disk: the pipeline file now ends with a line
nobody from the toolbox wrote.
When the developer reloads the framework
One command. It re-applies the project's own answers, then redoes the GitLab setup from
scratch: it revokes both automation tokens and creates new ones, even though they still
worked, and resets the branch protection.
Then the framework file is back to what the toolbox ships
The pipeline file is back to the bytes the toolbox ships — the hand-written line is gone.
And the default branch is locked down again
The default branch is strict again: no one may push to it, maintainers may merge.
